title: The Normativity of Meaning and Content

summaries.example: Imagine that your class uses the word “triangle” for a shape with three sides. If someone uses it for a circle, the use does not fit the word’s meaning. Philosophers ask whether this mismatch is merely a fact about language, or whether it also means the speaker ought to use the word differently. They also ask whether the rules for using “triangle” help create its meaning in the first place.
summaries.summary: This entry explores the idea that meaning and mental content may be normative. “Normative” means connected with standards about what is correct, permitted, valuable, or required. One kind of theory says that having a meaning gives us standards for using words or concepts. Another kind says that rules or norms help determine what words and thoughts mean. The first kind is called meaning- or content-engendered normativity; the second is meaning- or content-determining normativity. The discussion also separates ordinary rules for reaching a goal from rules that help constitute an activity, such as game rules. Philosophers debate whether semantic correctness really brings an “ought,” whether rules guide speakers, and whether rule-based explanations lead to a never-ending chain of further rules. Related arguments concern belief and truth. Some philosophers think beliefs are governed by a truth standard, while others say that any such standard may come from our goals or from other kinds of rules. The entry concludes that there is no broad agreement yet, including on whether meaning and content can be explained entirely in natural, non-normative terms.
key_ideas: The entry asks whether meaning and thought are connected to rules about how words and ideas should be used.
One view says meaning creates standards for correct use. Another says rules help create meaning.
A word can be used incorrectly even when the speaker understands what the word means.
Philosophers disagree about whether these standards are real norms or only ways of sorting uses into right and wrong.
Similar questions arise for beliefs: does having a belief include a rule to believe what is true?
The entry does not settle the debate; it explains the main arguments on both sides.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use words and form beliefs constantly. Understanding this debate helps us see why language is more than making noises and why mistakes in speaking or thinking can matter. It also shows how philosophers examine an everyday idea—“that is the right word” or “you should believe what is true”—by asking what makes it true and what kind of rule is involved.

important_terms.definition: A rule or standard about what someone should do, may do, or should avoid doing.
What a word, sentence, or thought stands for or communicates.
The idea that something is right or wrong according to a standard.
A rule that helps make an activity what it is, like rules that make chess a game.

questions_to_think_about: Is using a word incorrectly the same as breaking a rule?
Can a game exist without rules? Could a language exist without rules?
If a person says something false, did they use the words wrongly, or did they simply make a mistake about the world?
Should people believe every true thing, even things they have no way to discover?

summaries.example: Suppose a student uses “green” to describe a red traffic light. One philosopher may say that because “green” means green, the student ought to apply it only to green things. An opponent may agree that the application is false or semantically incorrect but deny that this fact alone creates an obligation. The disagreement is about whether semantic correctness is itself normative, or whether it merely classifies applications by their truth conditions.
summaries.summary:
The entry examines normativism about linguistic meaning and intentional or mental content. The thesis is not a single doctrine, because both “normativity” and the claim that it is essential to meaning can be understood in different ways. The most important division concerns explanatory direction. Meaning- or content-engendered normativity claims that once an expression or mental state has a meaning or content, normative consequences follow. Meaning- or content-determining normativity claims that norms are part of what makes meaning or content possible and may determine which meaning or content something has. The latter is therefore a thesis in metaphysics or foundational semantics, not merely a claim about how people talk.

For meaning-engendered normativity, a famous strategy begins with correctness conditions. If “green” means green, then applying it to green objects is semantically correct. The normativist argues that this supports an obligation or permission concerning use. The anti-normativist replies that correctness may simply sort applications into true and false, without prescribing behavior. Other proposals appeal to using an expression in accordance with its meaning, to commitments arising from participation in a rule-governed practice, or to the prescriptive role of meaning statements. Each proposal faces questions about whether its norms are genuinely semantic rather than pragmatic or instrumental.

Meaning-determining normativism instead asks what makes an expression have a meaning at all. Rules of use, conventions, rational dispositions, biological functions, and principles of interpretation have all been considered. key_ideas: The central metaphysical question is whether norms explain meaning and content, or whether meaning and content generate normative consequences.
The simple argument moves from the existence of semantic correctness conditions to claims about what speakers ought to do. Critics argue that “correct” can be descriptive rather than normative.
A speaker can make an empirical mistake while using a word in accordance with its meaning; this distinguishes linguistic error from error about the world.
Meaning-determining theories often appeal to rules of use, conventions, rational dispositions, or interpretation principles, but they must explain how such rules are in force.
Rule-guidance raises a regress problem: if following a rule requires another thought or rule, it may seem that explanation never reaches a basic level.

Content normativism extends the debate to beliefs and concepts, especially the proposed truth norm of belief. That proposal faces worries about impossible demands and about whether truth guides belief formation.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue connects ordinary linguistic mistakes with deep questions about explanation. If meaning carries standards, then language may involve more than patterns of behavior or causal facts. If it does not, philosophers must explain why semantic criticism and correction seem so natural. The debate also affects theories of thought, belief, rationality, and naturalism. It teaches a broader philosophical lesson: an apparently simple word such as “correct” may have both descriptive and normative uses, and arguments can depend on which use is intended.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical idea that meaning or mental content is essentially connected with norms, standards, or reasons.
Normativity that follows from an already existing meaning or content, without saying how that meaning or content was established.
The view that norms or rules are metaphysically prior and help constitute or determine meaning or content.
A standard concerning what is correct, incorrect, allowed, forbidden, valuable, or required.
A rule that does not merely regulate an activity but helps make that activity possible, as game rules help make a game the game it is.
A relation in which one set of facts determines another, while the determining principle still needs to be explained.
A theory of meaning or content that explains it entirely in terms of natural facts, such as behavior, dispositions, or causal processes.
The view that beliefs are subject to standards involving truth, justification, knowledge, or rational inference.

questions_to_think_about: Does calling an application of “green” correct already imply that the speaker should make that application?
Can a person use a word with its established meaning while holding a false belief about the object being discussed?
What makes a rule genuinely guide behavior rather than merely describe a regular pattern?
If belief is governed by a truth norm, how could that norm guide someone before they have already judged what is true?
Could meaning be explained by natural facts without losing the distinction between correct use and mere regular use?

summaries.example: A student knows that the classroom rule says “raise your hand before speaking,” but sometimes calls out anyway. In a game, breaking a rule can still be a move in the game: the move is illegal, but it is not outside the game. Philosophers use comparisons like this when asking about language. Can someone say something that is semantically wrong while still using the same word with the same meaning? If yes, then a rule may be in force even when a speaker does not follow it.
summaries.summary:
This entry studies a family of theories called normativism about meaning and content. Normativism says that meaning and mental content are essentially connected with norms, but philosophers disagree about what that connection is. A norm can concern action—what one ought to do, may do, or must not do—or it can concern value. The entry focuses mainly on action-guiding norms and distinguishes instrumental norms, which depend on a goal, from non-instrumental norms. It also discusses constitutive rules, which help create the activities they regulate, as game rules help make games possible.

The first major distinction is between engendered and determining normativity. Engendered normativity says that meaning or content has normative consequences. For example, if “green” means green, then applications of the word have semantic correctness conditions. A direct argument claims that this correctness entails that a speaker ought to use the word only in the correct way. Critics reply that “correct” can be used without prescribing anything: an application can be correct because it is true, while the speaker is not thereby obligated to make it. Further proposals appeal to using words in accordance with their meanings, commitments that arise from participating in linguistic practices, or the possible prescriptive role of meaning statements. These proposals must show that the normativity is semantic rather than merely practical, social, or connected to a desire to communicate.

Determining normativity makes a stronger explanatory claim. It says that rules or norms help constitute meaning. key_ideas: The debate has two directions: meanings may produce norms, or norms may help produce meanings.
Supporters of the “simple argument” say that if a word has a meaning, it has correct and incorrect applications, and this seems to create standards for speakers.
Critics distinguish descriptive correctness, such as being true, from normative correctness, which says what someone should do.
Rules can be constitutive. Chess rules do not merely tell players how to move; they help make an activity chess. Some philosophers think language works similarly.
A major challenge for rule theories is explaining how rules guide people without requiring another rule to explain how the first rule is followed.
The debate about mental content includes the question whether beliefs have an essential standard of truth, or whether truth matters only because people have certain goals.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate helps explain why language and thought seem answerable to standards. We distinguish a word used wrongly from a sound that has no meaning, and we distinguish a mistaken belief from a random mental event. Philosophers ask whether these distinctions require genuine norms or can be explained in non-normative ways. The issue therefore reaches beyond vocabulary: it concerns reasoning, belief, social practices, and whether naturalistic theories can capture everything important about meaning.

important_terms.definition: A standard that tells us what is correct, required, allowed, forbidden, or valuable.
The idea that meaning or thought content is essentially tied to standards for correct use or thought.
Normativity that is produced by having a meaning or content; it does not by itself say how that meaning or content was fixed.
Normativity in which rules or norms help determine what an expression means or what a thought is about.
A rule that helps create an activity or status, rather than merely controlling an activity that already exists.
A statement of the conditions under which a word or thought counts as correct or incorrect.
A problem in which explaining one rule-guided action requires another rule or thought, apparently continuing without a starting point.
A philosophical view that tries to explain meaning or content through natural facts, such as behavior, dispositions, or functions.

questions_to_think_about: When someone uses a word incorrectly, are they breaking a semantic rule or just saying something false?
Can a rule be in force even when people do not consciously know or accept it?
Why might rules of language be different from ordinary advice, such as “study if you want a good grade”?
Does a truth standard tell us what to believe, or does it only evaluate beliefs after we have formed them?
What would a theory of meaning lose if it explained language only through patterns of behavior?
